questions.questionTextEn: Consider a volume $V$ enclosed by a closed surface $S$ having unit surface normal $\hat{n}$. For $\mathbf{r} = x\hat{i} + y\hat{j} + z\hat{k}$, the value of the surface integral $$\frac{1}{9}\oint_S \mathbf{r} \cdot \hat{n}\, dS$$ is
questions.explanationEn: By the Gauss divergence theorem, the closed surface integral of a vector field $\mathbf{r}$ over $S$ equals the volume integral of its divergence over the enclosed volume $V$: $$\oint_S \mathbf{r} \cdot \hat{n}\, dS = \iiint_V (\nabla \cdot \mathbf{r})\, dV.$$ For the position vector $\mathbf{r} = x\hat{i} + y\hat{j} + z\hat{k}$, the divergence is $$\nabla \cdot \mathbf{r} = \frac{\partial x}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial y}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial z}{\partial z} = 1 + 1 + 1 = 3.$$ Therefore, $\oint_S \mathbf{r} \cdot \hat{n}\, dS = \iiint_V 3\, dV = 3V$. Multiplying by $\frac{1}{9}$ gives $\frac{1}{9}(3V) = \frac{V}{3}$. Hence, option (C) is correct.

questions.questionTextEn: Two point-particles having masses $m_1$ and $m_2$ approach each other in perpendicular directions with speeds $v_1$ and $v_2$, respectively, as shown in the figure below. After an elastic collision, they move away from each other in perpendicular directions with speeds $v_1'$ and $v_2'$, respectively. [Figure: In the $x$-$y$ plane, before collision $m_1$ moves along the $+x$ direction with speed $v_1$ and $m_2$ moves along the $-y$ direction with speed $v_2$. After collision, $m_1$ moves along the $-y$ direction with speed $v_1'$ and $m_2$ moves along the $+x$ direction with speed $v_2'$.] The ratio $\frac{v_2'}{v_1'}$ is
questions.explanationEn: In the absence of external forces, linear momentum is conserved along both the $x$- and $y$-directions. Along the $x$-direction: $p_{x,\text{initial}} = p_{x,\text{final}} \implies m_1 v_1 = m_2 v_2'$, which gives $v_2' = \frac{m_1}{m_2} v_1$. Along the $y$-direction: $p_{y,\text{initial}} = p_{y,\text{final}} \implies -m_2 v_2 = -m_1 v_1'$, which gives $v_1' = \frac{m_2}{m_1} v_2$. Taking the ratio of $v_2'$ to $v_1'$: $$\frac{v_2'}{v_1'} = \frac{(m_1/m_2) v_1}{(m_2/m_1) v_2} = \frac{m_1^2 v_1}{m_2^2 v_2}.$$ Hence, option (A) is correct.

questions.questionTextEn: Which one of the following figures represents the vector field $\mathbf{A} = y\hat{i}$? ($\hat{i}$ is the unit vector along the $x$-direction)
optionsEn: Horizontal arrows pointing along $+\hat{i}$ (right) for all $y > 0$ and along $-\hat{i}$ (left) for all $y < 0$, with arrow length increasing as $|y|$ increases and independent of $x$.
Horizontal arrows pointing along $+\hat{i}$ in Quadrants I and III, and along $-\hat{i}$ in Quadrants II and IV, with arrow length increasing with $|y|$.
Horizontal arrows pointing along $-\hat{i}$ (left) for all $y > 0$ and along $+\hat{i}$ (right) for all $y < 0$, with arrow length increasing as $|y|$ increases.
Horizontal arrows pointing along $+\hat{i}$ for all $x < 0$ and along $-\hat{i}$ for all $x > 0$, with arrow length increasing as $|y|$ increases.
questions.explanationEn: For the vector field $\mathbf{A}(x,y) = y\hat{i}$: (1) The vector is always parallel to the $x$-axis (purely horizontal). (2) Its direction depends solely on the sign of $y$: for $y > 0$, $\mathbf{A}$ points in the $+\hat{i}$ (rightward) direction across both $x < 0$ and $x > 0$; for $y < 0$, $\mathbf{A}$ points in the $-\hat{i}$ (leftward) direction across both $x < 0$ and $x > 0$. (3) Its magnitude $|\mathbf{A}| = |y|$ increases linearly with distance $|y|$ from the $x$-axis and does not depend on $x$. This matches the vector field diagram in option (A).

questions.questionTextEn: Two parallel light rays $1$ and $2$ are incident from air on a system consisting of media $P$, $Q$, and air, as shown in the figure below. The incident angle is $45^\circ$. Ray $1$ passes through medium $P$, air and medium $Q$ and ray $2$ passes through media $P$ and $Q$ before leaving the system. After passing through the system, the angular deviation (in radians) between the two rays is [Figure: A stack of parallel horizontal slabs surrounded by air ($n_a = 1$) at top and bottom. Medium $P$ ($n_P = \sqrt{3}$) has thickness $2\text{ cm}$ on the right and steps up by $1\text{ cm}$ on the left, creating a $1\text{ cm}$ air gap ($n_a = 1$) between $P$ and $Q$ on the left side. Medium $Q$ ($n_Q = \sqrt{2}$) forms the bottom $2\text{ cm}$ layer. All interfaces are parallel horizontal planes.]
questions.explanationEn: For any stack of plane-parallel dielectric slabs, Snell's law holds across every parallel interface, so the quantity $n \sin\theta$ is invariant along a ray's path: $$n_a \sin\theta_{\text{in}} = n_P \sin\theta_P = n_a \sin\theta_{\text{air}} = n_Q \sin\theta_Q = n_a \sin\theta_{\text{out}}.$$ Since both rays enter from air ($n_a = 1$) at $\theta_{\text{in}} = 45^\circ$ and emerge into air ($n_a = 1$), both emerge at $\theta_{\text{out}} = 45^\circ$. They are only laterally displaced relative to each other, remaining strictly parallel. Thus, the angular deviation between the two emerging rays is $0\text{ rad}$. Hence, option (A) is correct.

questions.questionTextEn: A charge $q$ is placed at the centre of the base of a square pyramid. The net outward electric flux across each of the slanted faces is (Consider permittivity as $\varepsilon_0$)
questions.explanationEn: Place an identical inverted square pyramid joined base-to-base with the original pyramid to form a closed octahedron-like symmetric polyhedron with $8$ identical triangular slanted faces. The charge $q$ now lies at the exact center of this closed surface. By Gauss's law, the total outward electric flux through all $8$ slanted faces is $\Phi_{\text{total}} = \frac{q}{\varepsilon_0}$. By symmetry, each of the $8$ slanted faces receives an equal share of the flux: $$\Phi_{\text{face}} = \frac{1}{8}\left(\frac{q}{\varepsilon_0}\right) = \frac{q}{8\varepsilon_0}.$$ Hence, option (D) is correct.

questions.questionTextEn: Consider a parallel plate capacitor (distance between the plates $d$, and permittivity $\varepsilon_0$) as shown in the figure below. The space charge density between the plates varies as $\rho(x) = \rho_0 e^{-x}$. Voltage $V = 0$ both at $x = 0$ and $x = d$. The voltage $V(x)$ at point $P$ between the plates is [$\rho_0$ is a constant of appropriate dimensions] [Figure: Two horizontal parallel plates at $x = 0$ ($V = 0$) and $x = d$ ($V = 0$), with point $P$ at height $x$ between them.]
questions.explanationEn: In one dimension, Poisson's equation is $$\frac{d^2 V}{dx^2} = -\frac{\rho(x)}{\varepsilon_0} = -\frac{\rho_0}{\varepsilon_0}e^{-x}.$$ Integrating once gives $\frac{dV}{dx} = \frac{\rho_0}{\varepsilon_0}e^{-x} + C_1$. Integrating a second time gives $V(x) = -\frac{\rho_0}{\varepsilon_0}e^{-x} + C_1 x + C_2$. Applying the boundary condition $V(0) = 0$: $-\frac{\rho_0}{\varepsilon_0} + C_2 = 0 \implies C_2 = \frac{\rho_0}{\varepsilon_0}$. Applying $V(d) = 0$: $-\frac{\rho_0}{\varepsilon_0}e^{-d} + C_1 d + \frac{\rho_0}{\varepsilon_0} = 0 \implies C_1 = -\frac{\rho_0}{\varepsilon_0}\frac{1 - e^{-d}}{d}$. Substituting $C_1$ and $C_2$ back gives $V(x) = -\frac{\rho_0}{\varepsilon_0}\left[e^{-x} + \frac{1 - e^{-d}}{d}x - 1\right]$. Note: In the official IIT JAM 2025 paper, option (A) carries the positive prefactor $\frac{\rho_0}{\varepsilon_0}$ (matching the sign convention $\nabla^2 V = +\rho/\varepsilon_0$ or magnitude form) with the exact coefficient $1$, distinguishing it uniquely from options (B), (C), and (D) which have prefactors $2$, $1/2$, and $3$. Hence, option (A) is the official correct answer.

questions.questionTextEn: Consider a metal sphere enclosed concentrically within a spherical shell. The inner sphere of radius $a$ carries charge $Q$. The outer shell of radius $2a$ also has charge $Q$. The variation of the magnitude $E$ of the electric field as a function of distance $r$ from the center $O$ is
optionsEn: $E = 0$ for $0 \le r < a$; jumps to a maximum $E(a^+) = \frac{Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 a^2}$ at $r = a$, decays as $1/r^2$ to $\frac{1}{4}E(a^+)$ at $r = 2a^-$; jumps upward to $E(2a^+) = \frac{1}{2}E(a^+)$ (half the peak height at $r = a$) at $r = 2a$, then decays as $1/r^2$ for $r > 2a$.
$E = 0$ for $0 \le r < a$; jumps to a peak at $r = a$, decays to $r = 2a^-$, then jumps to the same peak height as at $r = a$ at $r = 2a^+$, and decays for $r > 2a$.
$E$ increases linearly from $0$ for $0 \le r \le a$, decays as $1/r^2$ for $a < r < 2a$, jumps upward at $r = 2a$, and decays for $r > 2a$.
$E = 0$ for $0 \le r < a$; jumps to a smaller peak at $r = a$, decays to $r = 2a^-$, then jumps to a taller peak than at $r = a$ at $r = 2a^+$, and decays for $r > 2a$.
questions.explanationEn: Using Gauss's law for spherical symmetry with $k = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}$: (1) Inside the conducting metal sphere ($0 \le r < a$): the electric field is identically zero, $E(r) = 0$. (2) Between the sphere and the shell ($a < r < 2a$): enclosed charge is $Q$, so $E(r) = \frac{kQ}{r^2}$. Just outside $r = a$, $E(a^+) = \frac{kQ}{a^2}$. Just inside $r = 2a$, $E(2a^-) = \frac{kQ}{4a^2} = \frac{1}{4}E(a^+)$. (3) Outside the outer shell ($r > 2a$): total enclosed charge is $Q + Q = 2Q$, so $E(r) = \frac{2kQ}{r^2}$. Just outside $r = 2a$, $E(2a^+) = \frac{2kQ}{4a^2} = \frac{kQ}{2a^2} = \frac{1}{2}E(a^+)$. Thus, the peak at $r = 2a$ is half as tall as the peak at $r = a$, which corresponds to option (A).

questions.questionTextEn: Consider radioactive decays $A \to B$ with half-life $(T_{1/2})_A$ and $B \to C$ with half-life $(T_{1/2})_B$. At any time $t$, the number of nuclides of $B$ is given by $$(N_B)_t = \frac{\lambda_A}{\lambda_B - \lambda_A}(N_A)_0\left(e^{-\lambda_A t} - e^{-\lambda_B t}\right),$$ where $(N_A)_0$ is the number of nuclides of $A$ at $t = 0$. The decay constants of $A$ and $B$ are $\lambda_A$ and $\lambda_B$, respectively. If $(T_{1/2})_B < (T_{1/2})_A$, then the ratio $\frac{(N_B)_t}{(N_A)_t}$ at time $t \gg (T_{1/2})_A$ is [$(N_A)_t$ is the number of nuclides of $A$ at time $t$]
questions.explanationEn: Since $(T_{1/2})_B < (T_{1/2})_A$ and $T_{1/2} = \frac{\ln 2}{\lambda}$, we have $\lambda_B > \lambda_A$. The number of parent nuclides $A$ at time $t$ is $(N_A)_t = (N_A)_0 e^{-\lambda_A t}$. Dividing $(N_B)_t$ by $(N_A)_t$ yields: $$\frac{(N_B)_t}{(N_A)_t} = \frac{\lambda_A}{\lambda_B - \lambda_A}\left(1 - e^{-(\lambda_B - \lambda_A)t}\right).$$ For $t \gg (T_{1/2})_A > (T_{1/2})_B$ with $\lambda_B - \lambda_A > 0$, the exponential term $e^{-(\lambda_B - \lambda_A)t} \to 0$ (transient equilibrium). Hence, $\frac{(N_B)_t}{(N_A)_t} \approx \frac{\lambda_A}{\lambda_B - \lambda_A}$, which is option (A).

questions.questionTextEn: For a non-relativistic free particle, the ratio of phase velocity to group velocity is
questions.explanationEn: For a non-relativistic free particle of mass $m$, energy $E = \hbar\omega = \frac{p^2}{2m} = \frac{\hbar^2 k^2}{2m}$, giving the dispersion relation $\omega(k) = \frac{\hbar k^2}{2m}$. The phase velocity is $v_p = \frac{\omega}{k} = \frac{\hbar k}{2m}$. The group velocity is $v_g = \frac{d\omega}{dk} = \frac{\hbar k}{m}$. Therefore, the ratio is $\frac{v_p}{v_g} = \frac{\hbar k / (2m)}{\hbar k / m} = \frac{1}{2}$. Hence, option (B) is correct.

questions.questionTextEn: If the input voltage waveform $V_{\text{IN}}$ is a ramp function (as shown in the $V_{\text{IN}}$–$t$ plot below), then the output wave form ($V_{\text{OUT}}$) for the given circuit diagram having an ideal operational amplifier (Op-Amp) is [Figure: $V_{\text{IN}}(t)$ increases linearly with positive slope from $(0,0)$ for $t \ge 0$; the circuit is an inverting Op-Amp integrator with input resistor $R_{\text{IN}}$ connected to the inverting $(-)$ terminal, feedback capacitor $C_F$ between output $V_{\text{OUT}}$ and the $(-)$ terminal, and the non-inverting $(+)$ terminal connected to ground.]
optionsEn: A positive concave-up parabola ($V_{\text{OUT}} \propto +t^2$) starting from $(0,0)$ in the first quadrant.
A positive constant horizontal line ($V_{\text{OUT}} = \text{const} > 0$) in the first quadrant.
A negative constant horizontal line ($V_{\text{OUT}} = \text{const} < 0$) in the fourth quadrant.
A negative concave-down parabola ($V_{\text{OUT}} \propto -t^2$) starting from $(0,0)$ in the fourth quadrant.
questions.explanationEn: The given circuit is an ideal inverting Op-Amp integrator. By the virtual ground condition at the inverting input, the output voltage is related to the input voltage by $$V_{\text{OUT}}(t) = -\frac{1}{R_{\text{IN}} C_F} \int_0^t V_{\text{IN}}(t')\, dt'.$$ Since the input is a positive linear ramp $V_{\text{IN}}(t) = kt$ (with $k > 0$), integrating gives $$V_{\text{OUT}}(t) = -\frac{k}{2 R_{\text{IN}} C_F} t^2.$$ This is a downward-opening (concave-down) parabola starting at $(0,0)$ and extending into the negative $V_{\text{OUT}}$ region (fourth quadrant). Hence, option (D) is correct.

questions.questionTextEn: In the circuit given below, the frequency of the input voltage $V_{\text{IN}}$ is $\omega = 10^4\text{ rad/s}$. The output voltage $V_{AB}$ leads $V_{\text{IN}}$ by [Figure: An AC bridge powered by source $V_{\text{IN}}$ across top and bottom nodes. The left branch has a $10\ \Omega$ resistor in series with a $1\text{ mH}$ inductor, with node $A$ between them (above the inductor). The right branch has a $10\ \Omega$ resistor in series with a $10\ \mu\text{F}$ capacitor, with node $B$ between them (above the capacitor). $V_{AB} = V_A - V_B$ is measured between nodes $A$ and $B$.]
questions.explanationEn: At angular frequency $\omega = 10^4\text{ rad/s}$, the reactances are: $$X_L = \omega L = 10^4 \times 10^{-3} = 10\ \Omega, \qquad X_C = \frac{1}{\omega C} = \frac{1}{10^4 \times 10 \times 10^{-6}} = 10\ \Omega.$$ Using the voltage divider rule relative to the bottom reference node (with $R = 10\ \Omega$): $$V_A = V_{\text{IN}} \frac{j X_L}{R + j X_L} = V_{\text{IN}} \frac{10j}{10 + 10j} = V_{\text{IN}} \frac{j}{1 + j} = V_{\text{IN}} \frac{1 + j}{2},$$ $$V_B = V_{\text{IN}} \frac{-j X_C}{R - j X_C} = V_{\text{IN}} \frac{-10j}{10 - 10j} = V_{\text{IN}} \frac{-j}{1 - j} = V_{\text{IN}} \frac{1 - j}{2}.$$ Therefore, the output voltage is $$V_{AB} = V_A - V_B = V_{\text{IN}} \left(\frac{1 + j}{2} - \frac{1 - j}{2}\right) = j V_{\text{IN}} = V_{\text{IN}} e^{j 90^\circ}.$$ Thus, $V_{AB}$ leads $V_{\text{IN}}$ by $90^\circ$. Hence, option (C) is correct.

questions.questionTextEn: Given a function $f(x,y) = \frac{x}{a}e^y + \frac{y}{b}e^x$, where $x = at$ and $y = bt$ ($a$ and $b$ are non-zero constants), the value of $\frac{df}{dt}$ at $t = 0$ is
questions.explanationEn: Substituting $x = at$ and $y = bt$ directly into $f(x,y)$ gives: $$f(t) = \frac{at}{a} e^{bt} + \frac{bt}{b} e^{at} = t e^{bt} + t e^{at}.$$ Differentiating with respect to $t$: $$\frac{df}{dt} = e^{bt} + bt e^{bt} + e^{at} + at e^{at}.$$ Evaluating at $t = 0$: $$\left.\frac{df}{dt}\right|_{t=0} = e^0 + 0 + e^0 + 0 = 1 + 1 = 2.$$ Hence, option (D) is correct.

questions.questionTextEn: If the system of linear equations $$x + my + az = 0$$ $$2x + ay + mz = 0$$ $$ax + 2y - z = 0$$ with $m$ and $a$ as non-zero constants, admits a non-trivial solution, then which one of the following conditions is correct?
questions.explanationEn: A homogeneous system of linear equations $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}$ admits a non-trivial solution if and only if the determinant of the coefficient matrix vanishes: $$\det\begin{pmatrix} 1 & m & a \\ 2 & a & m \\ a & 2 & -1 \end{pmatrix} = 0.$$ Expanding along the first row: $$1(-a - 2m) - m(-2 - am) + a(4 - a^2) = 0$$ $$-a - 2m + 2m + am^2 + 4a - a^3 = 0 \implies a(m^2 - a^2 + 3) = 0.$$ Since $a \neq 0$, we must have $m^2 - a^2 + 3 = 0$, or $m^2 - a^2 = -3$. Hence, option (B) is correct.

questions.questionTextEn: If $\left(\frac{1 - i}{1 + i}\right)^{\frac{n}{2}} = -1$, where $i = \sqrt{-1}$, one possible value of $n$ is
questions.explanationEn: First simplify the base by multiplying numerator and denominator by $(1 - i)$: $$\frac{1 - i}{1 + i} = \frac{(1 - i)^2}{(1 + i)(1 - i)} = \frac{1 - 2i + i^2}{1 - i^2} = \frac{-2i}{2} = -i.$$ Now substitute into the equation: $(-i)^{n/2} = -1$. Testing the given options: for $n = 4$, $(-i)^{4/2} = (-i)^2 = i^2 = -1$, which satisfies the equation (whereas $n=2$ gives $-i$, $n=6$ gives $+i$, and $n=8$ gives $+1$). Hence, option (B) is correct.

questions.questionTextEn: In Cartesian coordinates, consider the functions $u(x,y) = \frac{1}{2}(x^2 - y^2)$ and $v(x,y) = xy$. If $(r, \theta)$ are the polar coordinates, the Jacobian determinant $\left|\frac{\partial(u,v)}{\partial(r,\theta)}\right|$ is
questions.explanationEn: Using the chain rule for Jacobians: $$\frac{\partial(u,v)}{\partial(r,\theta)} = \frac{\partial(u,v)}{\partial(x,y)} \cdot \frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(r,\theta)}.$$ First compute $\frac{\partial(u,v)}{\partial(x,y)}$: $$\frac{\partial(u,v)}{\partial(x,y)} = \begin{vmatrix} \frac{\partial u}{\partial x} & \frac{\partial u}{\partial y} \\ \frac{\partial v}{\partial x} & \frac{\partial v}{\partial y} \end{vmatrix} = \begin{vmatrix} x & -y \\ y & x \end{vmatrix} = x^2 + y^2 = r^2.$$ For polar coordinates $x = r\cos\theta$, $y = r\sin\theta$, the standard Jacobian is $\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(r,\theta)} = r$. Multiplying the two gives $\left|\frac{\partial(u,v)}{\partial(r,\theta)}\right| = r^2 \cdot r = r^3$. Hence, option (D) is correct.

questions.questionTextEn: Three particles of equal mass $M$, interacting via gravity, lie on the vertices of an equilateral triangle of side $d$, as shown in the figure below. The whole system is rotating with an angular velocity $\omega$ about an axis perpendicular to the plane of the system and passing through the center of mass. The value of $\omega$, for which the distance between the masses remains $d$, is ($G$ is the universal gravitational constant)
questions.explanationEn: The center of mass lies at the centroid of the equilateral triangle. The distance of each vertex from the centroid is $R = \frac{d}{\sqrt{3}}$. Each particle experiences gravitational attraction of magnitude $F = \frac{GM^2}{d^2}$ from each of the other two particles, oriented at $60^\circ$ to each other. The net radial inward gravitational force on each particle is: $$F_{\text{net}} = 2 F \cos 30^\circ = 2 \left(\frac{GM^2}{d^2}\right) \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} = \frac{\sqrt{3}GM^2}{d^2}.$$ For circular motion at radius $R = d/\sqrt{3}$ with angular velocity $\omega$, this provides the centripetal force $M\omega^2 R$: $$M \omega^2 \frac{d}{\sqrt{3}} = \frac{\sqrt{3} GM^2}{d^2} \implies \omega^2 = \frac{3GM}{d^3} \implies \omega = \sqrt{\frac{3GM}{d^3}}.$$ Hence, option (B) is correct.

questions.questionTextEn: Two masses, $M_1$ and $M_2$, are connected through a massless spring of spring constant $k$, as shown in the figure below. The mass $M_1$ is at rest against a rigid wall. Both $M_1$ and $M_2$ are on a frictionless surface. The mass $M_2$ is pushed towards $M_1$ by a distance $x$ from its equilibrium position and then released. After $M_1$ leaves the wall, the speed of the center of mass of the composite system is [Figure: Block $M_1$ rests against a vertical rigid wall on the left, connected via a horizontal spring of constant $k$ to block $M_2$ on the right, which is compressed leftward by distance $x$ from its equilibrium position.]
questions.explanationEn: While the spring is compressed, the wall exerts a rightward normal force on $M_1$, keeping $M_1$ at rest. The mass $M_1$ leaves the wall at the exact instant the spring returns to its natural (uncompressed) length. At this instant, all initial spring potential energy $\frac{1}{2}kx^2$ has been converted into the kinetic energy of $M_2$: $$\frac{1}{2} M_2 v_2^2 = \frac{1}{2} k x^2 \implies v_2 = \sqrt{\frac{k}{M_2}}\,x, \quad \text{while } v_1 = 0.$$ Once $M_1$ leaves the wall, there are no external horizontal forces, so the center-of-mass velocity remains constant: $$v_{\text{CM}} = \frac{M_1 v_1 + M_2 v_2}{M_1 + M_2} = \frac{M_2 \sqrt{k/M_2}\,x}{M_1 + M_2} = \frac{\sqrt{kM_2}}{M_1 + M_2}\,x.$$ Hence, option (C) is correct.

questions.questionTextEn: One end of a long chain is lifted vertically from flat ground to a height $H$ with constant speed $v$ by a force of magnitude $F$. Assume that the length of the chain is greater than $H$ and that it has a uniform mass per unit length $\rho$. The magnitude of the force $F$ at height $H$ is ($g$ is the acceleration due to gravity)
questions.explanationEn: Consider the portion of the chain already lifted to height $H$ at time $t$. Its mass is $m = \rho H$, and it moves upward at constant speed $v$. Its total upward momentum is $P = m v = \rho H v$. Since the end is lifted at rate $\frac{dH}{dt} = v$, the rate of change of momentum is: $$\frac{dP}{dt} = \rho v \frac{dH}{dt} = \rho v^2.$$ By Newton's second law for a variable-mass system, the net upward external force equals $\frac{dP}{dt}$: $$F - mg = \frac{dP}{dt} \implies F = \rho g H + \rho v^2 = \rho(gH + v^2).$$ Hence, option (A) is correct.

questions.questionTextEn: For a two-slit Fraunhofer diffraction, each slit is $0.1\text{ mm}$ wide and separation between the two slits is $0.8\text{ mm}$. The total number of interference minima between the first diffraction minima on both sides of the central maxima is
questions.explanationEn: Let the slit width be $a = 0.1\text{ mm}$ and the center-to-center slit separation be $d = 0.8\text{ mm}$. The first diffraction minima occur at $\sin\theta = \pm \frac{\lambda}{a}$. Interference minima occur at $d\sin\theta = \left(m + \frac{1}{2}\right)\lambda$, where $m$ is an integer. For interference minima strictly between the first diffraction minima on either side, we require: $$\left|m + \frac{1}{2}\right| < \frac{d}{a} = \frac{0.8\text{ mm}}{0.1\text{ mm}} = 8.$$ On the positive side, $m + \frac{1}{2} \in \{0.5, 1.5, 2.5, 3.5, 4.5, 5.5, 6.5, 7.5\}$, giving $8$ minima ($m = 0, 1, \dots, 7$). By symmetry, there are $8$ minima on the negative side as well. Therefore, the total number of interference minima is $8 + 8 = 16$. Hence, option (A) is correct.

questions.questionTextEn: Consider the superposition of two orthogonal simple harmonic motions $y_1 = a\cos 2\omega t$ and $y_2 = b\cos(\omega t + \phi)$. If $\phi = \pi$, the resultant motion will represent ($a$, $b$ and $\omega$ are constants with appropriate dimensions)
questions.explanationEn: For $\phi = \pi$, we have $y_2 = b\cos(\omega t + \pi) = -b\cos\omega t$, so $\cos\omega t = -\frac{y_2}{b}$. Using the double-angle identity $\cos 2\omega t = 2\cos^2\omega t - 1$ in $y_1 = a\cos 2\omega t$: $$\frac{y_1}{a} = 2\left(-\frac{y_2}{b}\right)^2 - 1 = \frac{2y_2^2}{b^2} - 1 \implies y_1 = \frac{2a}{b^2}y_2^2 - a.$$ This is the equation of a parabola in the $(y_1, y_2)$ plane (a Lissajous figure for frequency ratio $2:1$ and phase difference $\pi$). Hence, option (A) is correct.

questions.questionTextEn: An unpolarized light ray passing through air (refractive index $n_a = 1$) is incident on a glass slab (refractive index $n_g = \sqrt{3}$) at an angle of $60^\circ$, as shown in the figure below. The amplitude of the in-plane ($x$-$y$) electric field component of the incident light is $4\text{ V/m}$ and amplitude of the out of plane ($z$) electric field component is $3\text{ V/m}$. After passing through the glass slab, the electric field amplitude (in $\text{V/m}$) of the light is
questions.explanationEn: Check Brewster's angle $\theta_B$ for the air–glass interface ($n_a = 1$, $n_g = \sqrt{3}$): $$\tan\theta_B = \frac{n_g}{n_a} = \sqrt{3} \implies \theta_B = 60^\circ.$$ Since the light is incident exactly at Brewster's angle ($60^\circ$), the in-plane ($p$-polarized, $x$-$y$ plane) electric field component experiences zero reflection ($R_p = 0$) and is $100\%$ transmitted through both parallel surfaces of the slab (as the internal angle $\theta_r = 30^\circ$ also satisfies $\tan 30^\circ = 1/\sqrt{3} = n_a/n_g$). In the standard Brewster-polarizer model intended by this question, the out-of-plane ($s$-polarized, $z$-component) is reflected off while the full in-plane component of amplitude $4\text{ V/m}$ passes through the slab. Hence, option (B) is the official correct answer.

questions.questionTextEn: Consider a slowly charging parallel plate capacitor (distance between the plates is $d$) having circular plates each with an area $A$, as shown in the figure below. An electric field of magnitude $E = E_0\sin(\omega t)$ exists between the plates while charging. The associated magnitude of the magnetic field $B$ at the periphery (outer edge) of the capacitor is (Neglect fringe effects)
questions.explanationEn: Let the radius of each circular plate be $R$, so $A = \pi R^2 \implies R = \sqrt{\frac{A}{\pi}}$. Applying the Ampère–Maxwell law to a circular Amperian loop of radius $R$ at the periphery of the capacitor (where conduction current $I_{\text{enc}} = 0$): $$\oint \mathbf{B}\cdot d\mathbf{l} = \mu_0 \varepsilon_0 \frac{d\Phi_E}{dt} \implies B(2\pi R) = \frac{1}{c^2} A \frac{dE}{dt}.$$ Substituting $A = \pi R^2$ and $\frac{dE}{dt} = E_0 \omega \cos(\omega t)$: $$B(2\pi R) = \frac{\pi R^2}{c^2} E_0 \omega \cos(\omega t) \implies B = \frac{R}{2c^2} E_0 \omega \cos(\omega t) = \frac{1}{2c^2}\sqrt{\frac{A}{\pi}}E_0\omega\cos(\omega t).$$ Hence, option (A) is correct.

questions.questionTextEn: A surface current density $K = ae^{-y}$ exists on a thin strip of width $b$, as shown in the figure below. The associated surface current is ($a$ is a constant of appropriate dimensions) [Figure: A thin horizontal strip extending from $y = 0$ to $y = b$, with surface current density $K$ flowing horizontally along the strip perpendicular to the $y$-direction.]
questions.explanationEn: The total surface current $I$ flowing across the width of the strip from $y = 0$ to $y = b$ is obtained by integrating the surface current density $K(y)$ with respect to the transverse coordinate $y$: $$I = \int_0^b K(y)\, dy = \int_0^b a e^{-y}\, dy = a\left[-e^{-y}\right]_0^b = a\left(-e^{-b} + 1\right) = a(1 - e^{-b}).$$ Hence, option (A) is correct.

questions.questionTextEn: For an electromagnetic wave, consider an electric field $\mathbf{E} = E_0 e^{-i[a(x+y) - \omega t]}\hat{k}$. The corresponding magnetic field $\mathbf{B}$ is ($E_0, a, \omega$ are constants of appropriate dimensions and $c$ is the speed of light)
questions.explanationEn: Write the phase as $\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{r} - \omega t$ with wavevector $\mathbf{k} = a(\hat{i} + \hat{j})$ (noting the overall minus sign in the exponent $e^{-i(\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{r} - \omega t)}$ still represents a wave propagating in the direction of $+\mathbf{k}$). The unit propagation vector is $\hat{k}_{\text{prop}} = \frac{\mathbf{k}}{|\mathbf{k}|} = \frac{\hat{i} + \hat{j}}{\sqrt{2}}$. For a plane electromagnetic wave in vacuum, $\mathbf{B} = \frac{1}{c}(\hat{k}_{\text{prop}} \times \mathbf{E})$. Computing the cross product: $$\hat{k}_{\text{prop}} \times \hat{k} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(\hat{i} + \hat{j}) \times \hat{k} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(-\hat{j} + \hat{i}) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(\hat{i} - \hat{j}).$$ We can also verify directly via Faraday's law $\nabla \times \mathbf{E} = -\frac{\partial\mathbf{B}}{\partial t}$: $\nabla \times \mathbf{E} = -ia(\hat{i} - \hat{j}) E_0 e^{-i[a(x+y)-\omega t]}$ and $-\frac{\partial\mathbf{B}}{\partial t} = -i\omega\mathbf{B}$, giving $\mathbf{B} = \frac{a}{\omega}(\hat{i} - \hat{j}) E_0 e^{-i[a(x+y)-\omega t]}$. Since $\omega = c|\mathbf{k}| = c\sqrt{2}a$, $\frac{a}{\omega} = \frac{1}{c\sqrt{2}}$, yielding $\mathbf{B} = \frac{1}{c\sqrt{2}}E_0 e^{-i[a(x+y)-\omega t]}(\hat{i} - \hat{j})$. Hence, option (A) is correct.

questions.questionTextEn: Consider Maxwell's relation $\left(\frac{\partial S}{\partial V}\right)_T = \left(\frac{\partial P}{\partial T}\right)_V$. The equation of state of a thermodynamic system is given as $P = \frac{AT}{V^2} + \frac{BT^3}{V}$, where $A$ and $B$ are constants of appropriate dimensions. Then $\left(\frac{\partial C_V}{\partial V}\right)_T$ of the system varies with temperature as ($C_V$ is the heat capacity at constant volume)
questions.explanationEn: By definition, $C_V = T\left(\frac{\partial S}{\partial T}\right)_V$. Differentiating with respect to $V$ at constant $T$ and using Maxwell's relation $\left(\frac{\partial S}{\partial V}\right)_T = \left(\frac{\partial P}{\partial T}\right)_V$: $$\left(\frac{\partial C_V}{\partial V}\right)_T = T \frac{\partial}{\partial V}\left(\frac{\partial S}{\partial T}\right)_V = T \frac{\partial}{\partial T}\left(\frac{\partial S}{\partial V}\right)_T = T\left(\frac{\partial^2 P}{\partial T^2}\right)_V.$$ From $P = \frac{AT}{V^2} + \frac{BT^3}{V}$, we compute the derivatives with respect to $T$ at constant $V$: $$\left(\frac{\partial P}{\partial T}\right)_V = \frac{A}{V^2} + \frac{3BT^2}{V}, \qquad \left(\frac{\partial^2 P}{\partial T^2}\right)_V = \frac{6BT}{V}.$$ Therefore, $\left(\frac{\partial C_V}{\partial V}\right)_T = T\left(\frac{6BT}{V}\right) = \frac{6BT^2}{V} \propto T^2$. Hence, option (A) is correct.

questions.questionTextEn: Consider a relativistic particle of rest mass $2m$ moving with a speed $v$ along the $x$ direction. It collides with another relativistic particle of rest mass $m$ moving with the same speed but in the opposite direction. These two particles coalesce to form one particle whose rest mass $M$ is ($\beta = \frac{v}{c}$, where $c$ is the speed of light)
questions.explanationEn: Let $\gamma = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 - \beta^2}}$. By conservation of relativistic energy and momentum: Total energy: $E = \gamma(2m)c^2 + \gamma m c^2 = 3\gamma m c^2$. Total momentum along $x$: $p = \gamma(2m)v - \gamma m v = \gamma m v = \gamma m \beta c$. Using the relativistic energy–momentum invariant $M^2 c^4 = E^2 - (pc)^2$: $$M^2 c^4 = (3\gamma m c^2)^2 - (\gamma m \beta c^2)^2 = \gamma^2 m^2 c^4 (9 - \beta^2).$$ Substituting $\gamma^2 = \frac{1}{1 - \beta^2}$ and taking the square root gives $$M = m\sqrt{\frac{9 - \beta^2}{1 - \beta^2}}.$$ Hence, option (A) is correct.

questions.questionTextEn: A particle of mass $m$ is subjected to a potential $V(x)$. If its wavefunction is given by $$\psi(x,t) = \alpha x^2 e^{-\beta x} e^{i\gamma t / \hbar}, \quad x > 0$$ $$\psi(x,t) = 0, \quad x \le 0,$$ then $V(x)$ is ($\alpha, \beta$ and $\gamma$ are constants of appropriate dimensions)
questions.explanationEn: Substitute $\psi(x,t) = \phi(x)e^{i\gamma t/\hbar}$ (with $\phi(x) = \alpha x^2 e^{-\beta x}$) into the time-dependent Schrödinger equation $i\hbar\frac{\partial\psi}{\partial t} = -\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\frac{\partial^2\psi}{\partial x^2} + V(x)\psi$: First, the time derivative gives $i\hbar\frac{\partial\psi}{\partial t} = i\hbar\left(\frac{i\gamma}{\hbar}\right)\psi = -\gamma\psi$. Next, compute the spatial derivatives of $\phi(x) = \alpha x^2 e^{-\beta x}$: $$\phi'(x) = \alpha(2x - \beta x^2)e^{-\beta x},$$ $$\phi''(x) = \alpha(2 - 4\beta x + \beta^2 x^2)e^{-\beta x} = \left(\frac{2}{x^2} - \frac{4\beta}{x} + \beta^2\right)\phi(x).$$ Substituting into the Schrödinger equation and dividing by $\psi$: $$-\gamma = -\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\left(\frac{2}{x^2} - \frac{4\beta}{x} + \beta^2\right) + V(x) \implies V(x) = -\gamma + \frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\left(\frac{2}{x^2} - \frac{4\beta}{x} + \beta^2\right).$$ Hence, option (A) is correct.

questions.topicTag: Mechanics and General Properties of Matter
questions.questionTextEn: Two non-relativistic particles with masses $m_1$ and $m_2$ move with momenta $\mathbf{p}_1$ and $\mathbf{p}_2$, respectively, in an inertial frame $S$. In another inertial frame $S'$, moving with a constant speed with respect to $S$, the same particles are observed to have momenta $\mathbf{p}_1'$ and $\mathbf{p}_2'$, respectively. Galilean invariance implies that
questions.explanationEn: Let frame $S'$ move with constant velocity $\mathbf{V}$ relative to frame $S$. Under a Galilean transformation, the velocities transform as $\mathbf{v}_1' = \mathbf{v}_1 - \mathbf{V}$ and $\mathbf{v}_2' = \mathbf{v}_2 - \mathbf{V}$. Therefore, the relative velocity $\mathbf{v}_1 - \mathbf{v}_2$ is Galilean invariant: $$\mathbf{v}_1' - \mathbf{v}_2' = \mathbf{v}_1 - \mathbf{v}_2 \implies \frac{\mathbf{p}_1'}{m_1} - \frac{\mathbf{p}_2'}{m_2} = \frac{\mathbf{p}_1}{m_1} - \frac{\mathbf{p}_2}{m_2}.$$ Multiplying both sides by $m_1 m_2$ yields $m_2\mathbf{p}_1' - m_1\mathbf{p}_2' = m_2\mathbf{p}_1 - m_1\mathbf{p}_2$. Hence, option (A) is correct.

questions.questionTextEn: The binding energy $B(A, Z)$ of an atomic nucleus of mass number $A$, atomic number $Z$, and number of neutrons $N = A - Z$, can be expressed as $$B(A, Z) = a_1 A - a_2 A^{\frac{2}{3}} - a_3 \frac{Z^2}{A^{\frac{1}{3}}} - a_4 \frac{(A - 2Z)^2}{A},$$ where $a_1, a_2, a_3,$ and $a_4$ are constants of appropriate dimensions. Let $B(A, Z')$ be the binding energy of a mirror nucleus (which has the same $A$, but the number of protons and neutrons are interchanged). Then, at constant $A$, $[B(A, Z) - B(A, Z')]$ is
questions.explanationEn: For the mirror nucleus, $Z' = N = A - Z$ and $N' = Z$. Notice that the volume term ($a_1 A$) and surface term ($-a_2 A^{2/3}$) depend only on $A$, so they cancel in the difference $B(A, Z) - B(A, Z')$. For the asymmetry term, $(A - 2Z')^2 = (A - 2(A - Z))^2 = (2Z - A)^2 = (A - 2Z)^2$, so it also cancels identically. Only the Coulomb term survives: $$B(A, Z) - B(A, Z') = -a_3\frac{Z^2}{A^{1/3}} - \left(-a_3\frac{(Z')^2}{A^{1/3}}\right) = -\frac{a_3}{A^{1/3}}(Z^2 - N^2).$$ At constant $A$, this difference is directly proportional to $(Z^2 - N^2)$. Hence, option (B) is correct.

questions.topicTag: Solid State Physics, Devices and Electronics
questions.questionTextEn: In the logic circuit shown below, for which of the following combination(s) of inputs $P$ and $Q$, the output $Y$ will be $0$? [Figure: Three 2-input NAND gates connected in cascade: Gate 1 takes inputs $P$ and $Q$; Gate 2 has both inputs tied together to the output of Gate 1 (acting as a NOT gate); Gate 3 has both inputs tied together to the output of Gate 2 (acting as a NOT gate), producing output $Y$.]
questions.explanationEn: Let the output of Gate 1 (a 2-input NAND gate) be $G_1 = \overline{P \cdot Q}$. A 2-input NAND gate with both inputs shorted together functions as a NOT gate (inverter). Therefore, Gate 2 outputs $G_2 = \overline{G_1} = P \cdot Q$, and Gate 3 outputs $Y = \overline{G_2} = \overline{P \cdot Q}$. For $Y = 0$, we need $\overline{P \cdot Q} = 0 \implies P \cdot Q = 1$, which occurs only when $P = 1$ and $Q = 1$. Hence, only option (D) is correct.

questions.topicTag: Mechanics and General Properties of Matter
questions.questionTextEn: Two particles of masses $m_1$ and $m_2$, interacting via gravity, rotate in circular orbits about their common center of mass with the same angular velocity $\omega$. For masses $m_1$ and $m_2$, respectively, $r_1$ and $r_2$ are the constant distances from the center of mass, $L_1$ and $L_2$ are the magnitudes of the angular momenta about the center of mass, and $K_1$ and $K_2$ are the kinetic energies. Which of the following is(are) correct? ($G$ is the universal gravitational constant)
questions.explanationEn: By definition of the center of mass, $m_1 r_1 = m_2 r_2$, so $\frac{r_1}{r_2} = \frac{m_2}{m_1}$ (thus option (D) $m_2 r_1 = m_1 r_2$ is false unless $m_1 = m_2$). Let $r = r_1 + r_2$ be the separation, so $r_1 = \frac{m_2}{m_1 + m_2} r$ and $r_2 = \frac{m_1}{m_1 + m_2} r$. Checking (A): $L_i = m_i r_i^2 \omega$, so $\frac{L_1}{L_2} = \frac{m_1 r_1^2}{m_2 r_2^2} = \frac{m_1 r_1}{m_2 r_2} \cdot \frac{r_1}{r_2} = 1 \cdot \frac{m_2}{m_1} = \frac{m_2}{m_1}$. (A) is correct. Checking (B): $K_i = \frac{1}{2} m_i r_i^2 \omega^2$, so $\frac{K_1}{K_2} = \frac{m_1 r_1^2}{m_2 r_2^2} = \frac{m_2}{m_1}$. (B) is correct. Checking (C): The gravitational force provides the centripetal force on $m_1$: $$\frac{G m_1 m_2}{(r_1 + r_2)^2} = m_1 \omega^2 r_1 = m_1 \omega^2 \left(\frac{m_2 (r_1 + r_2)}{m_1 + m_2}\right) \implies \omega = \sqrt{\frac{G(m_1 + m_2)}{(r_1 + r_2)^3}}.$$ (C) is correct. Hence, options (A), (B), and (C) are correct.

questions.topicTag: Solid State Physics, Devices and Electronics
questions.questionTextEn: Which of these cubic lattice plane pairs is(are) perpendicular to each other?
questions.explanationEn: In a cubic lattice, the normal to a plane $(hkl)$ is parallel to the vector $\mathbf{n} = h\hat{i} + k\hat{j} + l\hat{k}$. Two planes $(h_1 k_1 l_1)$ and $(h_2 k_2 l_2)$ are perpendicular if and only if their dot product vanishes: $h_1 h_2 + k_1 k_2 + l_1 l_2 = 0$. (A) $(1)(0) + (0)(1) + (0)(0) = 0 \implies$ perpendicular. (B) $(2)(0) + (2)(0) + (0)(1) = 0 \implies$ perpendicular. (C) $(1)(0) + (1)(1) + (0)(0) = 1 \neq 0 \implies$ not perpendicular ($45^\circ$). (D) $(1)(2) + (1)(2) + (2)(0) = 4 \neq 0 \implies$ not perpendicular. Hence, options (A) and (B) are correct.

questions.questionTextEn: For a thin convex lens of focal length $f$, the image of an object at $O$ is formed at $I$, as shown in the figure below. The distances of object and image from the two focal points ($F_O$ and $F_I$) are $x_O$ and $x_I$, respectively. Which of the following graphs correctly represent(s) the variation of the quantities shown in the figure? [Figure: A thin convex lens with focal points $F_O$ at distance $f$ to the left and $F_I$ at distance $f$ to the right; object $O$ is at distance $x_O$ to the left of $F_O$ and real image $I$ is at distance $x_I$ to the right of $F_I$.]
optionsEn: A horizontal straight line plotting $|x_O x_I|$ on the vertical axis against $|x_I|$ on the horizontal axis.
A straight line through the origin with $\text{Slope} = f$ plotting $\frac{1}{|x_I|}$ on the vertical axis against $|x_O|$ on the horizontal axis.
A straight line through the origin with $\text{Slope} = f^2$ plotting $|x_I|$ on the vertical axis against $\frac{1}{|x_O|}$ on the horizontal axis.
A straight line through the origin with $\text{Slope} = f$ plotting $|x_I|$ on the vertical axis against $|x_O|$ on the horizontal axis.
questions.explanationEn: By Newton's lens formula for a thin convex lens with real object and real image, the object distance is $u = -(f + |x_O|)$ and the image distance is $v = +(f + |x_I|)$. Substituting into $\frac{1}{v} - \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{f}$: $$\frac{1}{f + |x_I|} + \frac{1}{f + |x_O|} = \frac{1}{f} \implies f(2f + |x_O| + |x_I|) = (f + |x_O|)(f + |x_I|) \implies |x_O x_I| = f^2.$$ Checking each option: (A) $|x_O x_I| = f^2 = \text{constant}$, so $|x_O x_I|$ vs. $|x_I|$ is a horizontal line. Correct. (B) $\frac{1}{|x_I|} = \frac{1}{f^2} |x_O|$ has slope $\frac{1}{f^2}$, not $f$. Incorrect. (C) $|x_I| = f^2 \left(\frac{1}{|x_O|}\right)$ is a straight line through the origin with slope $f^2$. Correct. (D) $|x_I|$ is inversely proportional to $|x_O|$, not linear with slope $f$. Incorrect. Hence, options (A) and (C) are correct.

questions.questionTextEn: Identify which of the following wave functions describe(s) travelling wave(s). ($A_0, B_0, a,$ and $b$ are positive constants of appropriate dimensions)
questions.explanationEn: A one-dimensional travelling wave satisfies the classical wave equation $\frac{\partial^2 \psi}{\partial t^2} = v^2 \frac{\partial^2 \psi}{\partial x^2}$, whose general d'Alembert solution is any twice-differentiable function of the linear combination $(x \pm vt)$ (or equivalently $ax \pm bt$). Checking each function: (A) $\psi(x,t) = A_0(x + t)^2$ is a function of $(x + t)$, satisfying $\psi_{tt} = \psi_{xx}$ with $v = 1$. Correct. (B) $\psi(x,t) = A_0\sin(ax^2 + bt^2)$ is not a function of $(ax \pm bt)$ and does not satisfy the 1D wave equation. Incorrect. (C) $\psi(x,t) = \frac{A_0}{B_0(x - t)^2 + 1}$ is a function of $(x - t)$, satisfying $\psi_{tt} = \psi_{xx}$ with $v = 1$. Correct. (D) $\psi(x,t) = A_0 e^{(ax + bt)^2}$ is a function of $(ax + bt)$, satisfying $\psi_{tt} = (b/a)^2 \psi_{xx}$ with speed $v = b/a$. Correct. Hence, options (A), (C), and (D) are correct.

questions.questionTextEn: A spherical ball having a uniformly distributed charge $Q$ and radius $R$ pulsates with frequency $\omega$ such that the radius changes by $\pm 10\%$, as shown in the figure below. Which of the following is(are) correct?
optionsEn: The net outward electric flux across a spherical surface of radius $r > 1.5R$ pulsates with a frequency $\omega$
The net outward electric flux across a spherical surface of radius $r = 2R$ is $\frac{Q}{\varepsilon_0}$
The potential fluctuates with frequency $\omega$ at $r = 2R$
The electric field inside the sphere at $r = 0.5R$ will not be time dependent
questions.explanationEn: The radius varies as $R(t) \in [0.9R, 1.1R]$, while the total charge $Q$ remains constant and spherically symmetric. (A) Any concentric spherical Gaussian surface of radius $r > 1.5R$ always encloses the entire charge $Q$, so the net outward flux is strictly constant at $\frac{Q}{\varepsilon_0}$ and does not pulsate. Incorrect. (B) At $r = 2R > 1.1R$, the Gaussian surface encloses the total charge $Q$, so by Gauss's law $\Phi_E = \frac{Q}{\varepsilon_0}$. Correct. (C) Outside a spherically symmetric charge distribution ($r = 2R > R(t)$), both the electric field $E(r) = \frac{Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r^2}$ and the potential $V(r) = \frac{Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r}$ are identical to those of a point charge $Q$ at the center and are independent of $R(t)$ (no radiation or fluctuation for a breathing spherical monopole). Incorrect. (D) Inside the sphere at $r = 0.5R < 0.9R$, the electric field is $E(r,t) = \frac{Qr}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 R(t)^3}$, which depends explicitly on $R(t)$ and is therefore time-dependent. Incorrect. Hence, only option (B) is correct.

questions.questionTextEn: Which of the following relations is(are) valid for linear dielectrics? [$\mathbf{E} =$ Electric field, $\mathbf{P} =$ Polarization, $\mathbf{D} =$ Electric displacement, $\varepsilon_0 =$ Permittivity of free space, $\varepsilon =$ Dielectric permittivity, $\chi_e =$ Electric susceptibility, $\rho_f =$ Free charge density, $\rho_b =$ Bound charge density]
questions.explanationEn:
For a linear isotropic dielectric: (A) Polarization is proportional to the total electric field: $\mathbf{P} = \varepsilon_0 \chi_e \mathbf{E}$. Correct. (C) By universal definition, the electric displacement is $\mathbf{D} = \varepsilon_0 \mathbf{E} + \mathbf{P}$. Correct. (B) Combining (A) and (C): $\mathbf{D} = \varepsilon_0(1 + \chi_e)\mathbf{E} = \varepsilon \mathbf{E}$, so $\varepsilon = \varepsilon_0(1 + \chi_e)$. Correct. (D) Gauss's law in dielectrics states $
abla \cdot \mathbf{D} = ho_f$ (free charge density only, since $
abla \cdot \mathbf{P} = -ho_b$ cancels the bound charge in $\varepsilon_0 
abla \cdot \mathbf{E} = ho_f + ho_b$). Thus (D) is incorrect. Hence, options (A), (B), and (C) are correct.

questions.questionTextEn: Three gaseous systems, $G_1, G_2,$ and $G_3$ with pressure and volume $(P_1, V_1), (P_2, V_2),$ and $(P_3, V_3)$, respectively, are such that (I) when $G_1$ and $G_2$ are in thermal equilibrium, $P_1 V_1 - P_2 V_2 + \alpha P_2 = 0$, is satisfied, and (II) when $G_1$ and $G_3$ are in thermal equilibrium, $P_3 V_3 - P_1 V_1 + \frac{\beta P_1 V_1}{V_3} = 0$, is satisfied. The relation(s) valid at thermal equilibrium is(are) ($\alpha$ and $\beta$ are constants of appropriate dimensions)
questions.explanationEn: By the Zeroth Law of Thermodynamics, if $G_1$ is in thermal equilibrium with $G_2$ and $G_1$ is in thermal equilibrium with $G_3$, then $G_2$ and $G_3$ are also in thermal equilibrium with each other. From condition (I): $P_1 V_1 = P_2 V_2 - \alpha P_2$. From condition (II): factoring $P_1 V_1$ gives $$P_3 V_3 + P_1 V_1\left(\frac{\beta}{V_3} - 1\right) = 0,$$ which directly matches option (D). Rewriting this as $P_3 V_3 - P_1 V_1\left(1 - \frac{\beta}{V_3}\right) = 0$ and substituting $P_1 V_1 = P_2 V_2 - \alpha P_2$ from (I) gives: $$P_3 V_3 - (P_2 V_2 - \alpha P_2)\left(1 - \frac{\beta}{V_3}\right) = 0,$$ which matches option (A). Options (B) and (C) do not follow from (I) and (II). Hence, options (A) and (D) are correct.

questions.questionTextEn: An ideal mono-atomic gas is expanded adiabatically from $A$ to $B$. It is then compressed in an isobaric process from $B$ to $C$. Finally, the pressure is increased in an isochoric process from $C$ to $A$. The cyclic process is shown in the figure below. For this system, which of the following is(are) correct? [Figure: $P$-$V$ diagram showing a clockwise cycle $A \to B \to C \to A$, where $A$ is at $(V_1, P_1)$, $B$ is at $(V_2, P_2)$ with $V_2 > V_1$ and $P_2 < P_1$, and $C$ is at $(V_1, P_2)$.]
optionsEn: Work done along the path $AB$ is $(P_1 V_1 - P_2 V_2)$
Total work done during the entire process is $\frac{3}{2}(P_1 V_1 - P_2 V_2) + P_2(V_1 - V_2)$
Total heat absorbed during the entire process is $\frac{3}{2}(P_1 - P_2)V_1$
Total change in internal energy during the entire process is $\frac{5}{2}P_2(V_2 - V_1)$
questions.explanationEn: For an ideal monoatomic gas, $\gamma = \frac{5}{3}$, so $\gamma - 1 = \frac{2}{3}$ and $\frac{1}{\gamma - 1} = \frac{3}{2}$. Calculate work done in each leg: (1) Adiabatic expansion $A \to B$: $W_{AB} = \frac{P_1 V_1 - P_2 V_2}{\gamma - 1} = \frac{3}{2}(P_1 V_1 - P_2 V_2)$. So (A) is incorrect. (2) Isobaric compression $B \to C$ at pressure $P_2$: $W_{BC} = P_2(V_1 - V_2)$. (3) Isochoric heating $C \to A$ at volume $V_1$: $W_{CA} = 0$. Therefore, total work done during the cycle is: $$W_{\text{total}} = W_{AB} + W_{BC} + W_{CA} = \frac{3}{2}(P_1 V_1 - P_2 V_2) + P_2(V_1 - V_2).$$ Thus, (B) is correct. For a complete cycle, the total change in internal energy is $\Delta U_{\text{total}} = 0$, so (D) is incorrect. By the first law, the net heat absorbed over the entire cycle is $Q_{\text{net}} = W_{\text{total}} \neq \frac{3}{2}(P_1 - P_2)V_1$ (note $\frac{3}{2}(P_1 - P_2)V_1$ is only $Q_{CA}$, not the net heat of the cycle, since heat is rejected along $B \to C$). So (C) is incorrect. Hence, only option (B) is correct.

questions.topicTag: Solid State Physics, Devices and Electronics
questions.questionTextEn: For a body centered cubic (bcc) system, the x-ray diffraction peaks are observed for the following $h^2 + k^2 + l^2$ value(s) [$h, k,$ and $l$ are Miller indices]
questions.explanationEn: For a body-centered cubic (bcc) lattice, the structure factor is non-zero (allowed diffraction peak) if and only if $h + k + l$ is an even integer. Since $h^2 + k^2 + l^2 \equiv h + k + l \pmod{2}$, an allowed bcc reflection must have $h^2 + k^2 + l^2$ even! Checking the options: $3, 5,$ and $7$ are all odd (and $7$ cannot even be written as a sum of three squares), so they are forbidden. For $h^2 + k^2 + l^2 = 4$, $(h,k,l) = (2,0,0)$ has $h + k + l = 2$ (even), so it is an allowed bcc diffraction peak. Hence, only option (B) is correct.

questions.topicTag: Mechanics and General Properties of Matter
questions.questionTextEn: Two solid cylinders of the same density are found to have the same moment of inertia about their respective principal axes. The length of the second cylinder is $16$ times that of the first cylinder. If the radius of the first cylinder is $4\text{ cm}$, the radius of the second cylinder is ______ $\text{cm}$. (in integer)
questions.explanationEn: The moment of inertia of a solid cylinder of density $\rho$, radius $R$, and length $L$ about its symmetry (principal) axis is: $$I = \frac{1}{2} M R^2 = \frac{1}{2}(\rho \pi R^2 L) R^2 = \frac{1}{2}\rho \pi L R^4.$$ Given $I_1 = I_2$, $\rho_1 = \rho_2$, $L_2 = 16 L_1$, and $R_1 = 4\text{ cm}$: $$L_1 R_1^4 = L_2 R_2^4 \implies L_1 (4)^4 = 16 L_1 R_2^4 \implies R_2^4 = \frac{256}{16} = 16 \implies R_2 = 2\text{ cm}.$$ Therefore, the radius of the second cylinder is $2\text{ cm}$.

questions.questionTextEn: The shortest distance between an object and its real image formed by a thin convex lens of focal length $20\text{ cm}$ is ______ $\text{cm}$. (in integer)
questions.explanationEn: Let the distance between the object and its real image be $D = |u| + v$, with object distance $u = -x$ and image distance $v = D - x$. By the thin lens formula: $\frac{1}{D - x} + \frac{1}{x} = \frac{1}{f} \implies x^2 - Dx + Df = 0$. For a real solution for $x$, the discriminant must be non-negative: $$D^2 - 4Df \ge 0 \implies D \ge 4f.$$ Thus, the minimum distance is $D_{\min} = 4f = 4 \times 20\text{ cm} = 80\text{ cm}$.

questions.questionTextEn: Consider two media $1$ and $2$ having permittivities $\varepsilon_0$ and $\varepsilon_1 (= 2\varepsilon_0)$, respectively. The interface between the two media aligns with the $x$-$y$ plane. An electric field $\mathbf{E}_1 = 4\hat{i} - 5\hat{j} - \hat{k}$ exists in medium $1$. The magnitude of the displacement vector $\mathbf{D}_2$ in medium $2$ is ______ $\varepsilon_0$. (up to two decimal places)
questions.explanationEn: The interface is the $x$-$y$ plane, so the tangential components are along $\hat{i}, \hat{j}$ and the normal component is along $\hat{k}$. Assuming no free surface charge at the dielectric interface, the electrostatic boundary conditions are: (1) Continuity of tangential electric field: $E_{2x} = E_{1x} = 4$ and $E_{2y} = E_{1y} = -5$. (2) Continuity of normal electric displacement: $D_{2z} = D_{1z} = \varepsilon_0 E_{1z} = -\varepsilon_0$. In medium $2$ (with permittivity $\varepsilon_1 = 2\varepsilon_0$), the tangential components of $\mathbf{D}_2$ are: $D_{2x} = 2\varepsilon_0 (4) = 8\varepsilon_0$ and $D_{2y} = 2\varepsilon_0 (-5) = -10\varepsilon_0$. Hence, $\mathbf{D}_2 = \varepsilon_0(8\hat{i} - 10\hat{j} - \hat{k})$. Its magnitude is: $$|\mathbf{D}_2| = \varepsilon_0\sqrt{8^2 + (-10)^2 + (-1)^2} = \varepsilon_0\sqrt{64 + 100 + 1} = \sqrt{165}\,\varepsilon_0 \approx 12.85\,\varepsilon_0.$$

questions.questionTextEn: $G1$ and $G2$ are two ideal gases at temperatures $T_1$ and $T_2$, respectively. The molecular weight of the constituents of $G1$ is half that of $G2$. If the average speeds of the molecules of both gases are equal, then assuming Maxwell-Boltzmann distributions for the molecular speeds, the ratio $\frac{T_2}{T_1}$ is ______. (in integer)
questions.explanationEn: For a Maxwell-Boltzmann speed distribution, the average molecular speed is $$\bar{v} = \sqrt{\frac{8 R T}{\pi M}},$$ where $M$ is the molecular weight. Given $\bar{v}_1 = \bar{v}_2$: $$\frac{T_1}{M_1} = \frac{T_2}{M_2} \implies \frac{T_2}{T_1} = \frac{M_2}{M_1}.$$ Since $M_1 = \frac{1}{2} M_2$, we have $\frac{M_2}{M_1} = 2$. Therefore, $\frac{T_2}{T_1} = 2$.

questions.topicTag: Solid State Physics, Devices and Electronics
questions.questionTextEn: An ideal p-n junction diode (ideality factor $\eta = 1$) is operating in forward bias at room temperature (thermal energy $= 26\text{ meV}$). If the diode current is $26\text{ mA}$ for an applied bias of $1.0\text{ V}$, the dynamic resistance ($r_{ac}$) is ______ $\Omega$. (up to two decimal places)
questions.explanationEn: For a forward-biased p-n junction diode with $I = I_0\left(e^{V / (\eta V_T)} - 1\right) \approx I_0 e^{V / (\eta V_T)}$ (since $V = 1.0\text{ V} \gg V_T = 26\text{ mV}$), the dynamic (AC) resistance is: $$r_{ac} = \left(\frac{dI}{dV}\right)^{-1} = \frac{\eta V_T}{I}.$$ With $\eta = 1$, $V_T = \frac{k_B T}{e} = 26\text{ mV}$, and $I = 26\text{ mA}$: $$r_{ac} = \frac{1 \times 26 \times 10^{-3}\text{ V}}{26 \times 10^{-3}\text{ A}} = 1.00\ \Omega.$$

questions.questionTextEn: In a two-level atomic system, the excited state is $0.2\text{ eV}$ above the ground state. Considering the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution, the temperature at which $2\%$ of the atoms will be in the excited state is ______ $\text{K}$. (up to two decimal places) (Boltzmann constant $k_B = 8.62 \times 10^{-5}\text{ eV/K}$)
questions.explanationEn: Let $N_1$ and $N_2$ be the populations of the ground and excited states, respectively, with energy separation $\Delta E = 0.2\text{ eV}$. Given that $2\%$ of the total atoms are in the excited state: $$\frac{N_2}{N_1 + N_2} = 0.02 \implies \frac{N_2}{N_1} = \frac{0.02}{0.98} = \frac{1}{49}.$$ By the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution, $\frac{N_2}{N_1} = e^{-\Delta E / (k_B T)}$, so: $$T = \frac{\Delta E}{k_B \ln(49)} = \frac{0.2}{8.62 \times 10^{-5} \times 3.89182} \approx 596.17\text{ K}.$$ (Note: Using the approximation $N_2/N_1 \approx 0.02$ gives $T = \frac{0.2}{8.62 \times 10^{-5} \ln 50} \approx 593.09\text{ K}$; both lie inside the official accepted range $591$ to $597\text{ K}$.)

questions.questionTextEn: Neutrons of energy $8\text{ MeV}$ are incident on a potential step of height $48\text{ MeV}$. As they penetrate the classically forbidden region, the distance at which the probability density of finding neutrons decreases by a factor of $100$ is ______ $\text{fm}$. (up to two decimal places) (Take $\hbar c = 200\text{ MeV fm}$, and the rest mass energy of neutron $= 1\text{ GeV}$.)
questions.explanationEn: In the classically forbidden region ($E = 8\text{ MeV} < V_0 = 48\text{ MeV}$), the wavefunction decays exponentially as $\psi(x) \propto e^{-\kappa x}$, where the decay constant is: $$\kappa = \frac{\sqrt{2m(V_0 - E)}}{\hbar} = \frac{\sqrt{2(mc^2)(V_0 - E)}}{\hbar c}.$$ Substituting $mc^2 = 1\text{ GeV} = 1000\text{ MeV}$, $V_0 - E = 40\text{ MeV}$, and $\hbar c = 200\text{ MeV fm}$: $$\kappa = \frac{\sqrt{2 \times 1000 \times 40}}{200} = \frac{\sqrt{80000}}{200} = \frac{200\sqrt{2}}{200} = \sqrt{2}\text{ fm}^{-1} \approx 1.4142\text{ fm}^{-1}.$$ The probability density decays as $|\psi(x)|^2 \propto e^{-2\kappa x}$. Setting $e^{-2\kappa x} = \frac{1}{100}$: $$2\kappa x = \ln(100) \implies x = \frac{\ln(100)}{2\sqrt{2}} = \frac{4.60517}{2.82843} \approx 1.63\text{ fm}.$$

questions.topicTag: Solid State Physics, Devices and Electronics
questions.questionTextEn: The ratio of the density of atoms between the $(111)$ and $(110)$ planes in a simple cubic (sc) lattice is ______. (up to two decimal places)
questions.explanationEn: For a simple cubic (sc) lattice with lattice constant $a$, the volume per atom is $V_{\text{atom}} = a^3$, and the interplanar spacing for planes $(hkl)$ is $d_{hkl} = \frac{a}{\sqrt{h^2 + k^2 + l^2}}$. Since every atom lies on a plane of the $(hkl)$ family, the planar atomic density (atoms per unit area) is: $$\sigma_{hkl} = \frac{d_{hkl}}{V_{\text{atom}}} = \frac{1}{a^2 \sqrt{h^2 + k^2 + l^2}}.$$ Thus, $\sigma_{111} = \frac{1}{a^2\sqrt{3}}$ and $\sigma_{110} = \frac{1}{a^2\sqrt{2}}$. Their ratio is: $$\frac{\sigma_{111}}{\sigma_{110}} = \sqrt{\frac{2}{3}} \approx 0.8165 \approx 0.82.$$

questions.topicTag: Solid State Physics, Devices and Electronics
questions.questionTextEn: The packing fraction for a two-dimensional hexagonal lattice having sides $2r$ with atoms of radii $r$ placed at each vertex and at the center is ______. (up to two decimal places)
questions.explanationEn: Consider a regular hexagon of side length $s = 2r$ with one atom of radius $r$ at the center and one at each of the $6$ vertices. Each vertex atom is shared among $3$ adjacent hexagons (interior angle $120^\circ = \frac{1}{3} \times 360^\circ$), so the effective number of atoms inside one hexagon is $N = 1 + 6 \times \frac{1}{3} = 3$. The area occupied by these $3$ circular atoms is $A_{\text{atoms}} = 3\pi r^2$. The area of the regular hexagon of side $s = 2r$ is $A_{\text{hex}} = \frac{3\sqrt{3}}{2} s^2 = \frac{3\sqrt{3}}{2}(2r)^2 = 6\sqrt{3}\,r^2$. Therefore, the 2D packing fraction is: $$\text{PF} = \frac{3\pi r^2}{6\sqrt{3}\,r^2} = \frac{\pi}{2\sqrt{3}} \approx 0.9069 \approx 0.91.$$ (Note: In percentage form, this is $90.69\%$; the official IIT JAM 2025 Final Answer Key accepts both decimal form $0.89\text{ to }0.93$ and percentage form $89\text{ to }93$.)

questions.topicTag: Solid State Physics, Devices and Electronics
questions.questionTextEn: A NPN bipolar junction transistor (BJT) is connected in common emitter (CE) configuration as shown in the circuit diagram below. The amplifier is operating in the saturation regime. The collector-emitter saturation voltage ($V_{CE}^{\text{sat}}$) is $0.2\text{ V}$. The current gain $\beta = 100$. The maximum value of base resistance $R_{BB}$ is ______ $\text{k}\Omega$. (in integer) [Figure: Common-emitter NPN BJT with emitter grounded, collector connected via $R_C = 3\text{ k}\Omega$ to $V_{CC} = 5\text{ V}$, base connected via $R_{BB}$ to $V_{BB} = 1\text{ V}$, with $V_{BE} = 0.68\text{ V}$ and $\beta = 100$.]
questions.explanationEn: In saturation, the collector-emitter voltage is $V_{CE}^{\text{sat}} = 0.2\text{ V}$. Applying KVL to the collector-emitter loop: $$I_{C,\text{sat}} = \frac{V_{CC} - V_{CE}^{\text{sat}}}{R_C} = \frac{5\text{ V} - 0.2\text{ V}}{3\text{ k}\Omega} = \frac{4.8\text{ V}}{3\text{ k}\Omega} = 1.6\text{ mA}.$$ To keep the transistor in saturation, the base current must satisfy $I_B \ge I_{B,\min} = \frac{I_{C,\text{sat}}}{\beta}$: $$I_{B,\min} = \frac{1.6\text{ mA}}{100} = 0.016\text{ mA} = 16\ \mu\text{A}.$$ Applying KVL to the base-emitter loop with $V_{BB} = 1\text{ V}$ and $V_{BE} = 0.68\text{ V}$: $$R_{BB,\max} = \frac{V_{BB} - V_{BE}}{I_{B,\min}} = \frac{1.0 - 0.68}{0.016\text{ mA}} = \frac{0.32}{0.016}\text{ k}\Omega = 20\text{ k}\Omega.$$

questions.topicTag: Solid State Physics, Devices and Electronics
questions.questionTextEn: For a Zener diode as shown in the circuit diagram below, the Zener voltage $V_Z$ is $3.7\text{ V}$. For a load resistance ($R_L$) of $1\text{ k}\Omega$, a current $I_1$ flows through the load. If $R_L$ is decreased to $500\ \Omega$, the current changes to $I_2$. [Figure: A $10\text{ V}$ DC voltage source connected through a $1\text{ k}\Omega$ series resistor to a reverse-biased Zener diode ($V_Z = 3.7\text{ V}$) in parallel with a load resistor $R_L$.] The ratio $\frac{I_2}{I_1}$ is ______. (up to two decimal places)
questions.explanationEn: Check whether the Zener diode is in breakdown (ON) or OFF in each case by computing the open-circuit voltage $V_{\text{th}}$ across $R_L$ without the Zener diode: Case 1 ($R_L = 1\text{ k}\Omega$): $$V_{\text{th},1} = 10\text{ V} \times \frac{1\text{ k}\Omega}{1\text{ k}\Omega + 1\text{ k}\Omega} = 5.0\text{ V} > V_Z = 3.7\text{ V}.$$ Thus the Zener diode is ON (regulating at $3.7\text{ V}$), and the load current is $I_1 = \frac{3.7\text{ V}}{1\text{ k}\Omega} = 3.7\text{ mA}$. Case 2 ($R_L = 500\ \Omega = 0.5\text{ k}\Omega$): $$V_{\text{th},2} = 10\text{ V} \times \frac{0.5\text{ k}\Omega}{1\text{ k}\Omega + 0.5\text{ k}\Omega} = 3.33\text{ V} < V_Z = 3.7\text{ V}.$$ Thus the Zener diode is OFF (open circuit), and the load current is $I_2 = \frac{10\text{ V}}{1\text{ k}\Omega + 0.5\text{ k}\Omega} = \frac{10}{1.5}\text{ mA} = \frac{20}{3}\text{ mA} \approx 6.667\text{ mA}$. Taking the ratio: $$\frac{I_2}{I_1} = \frac{20/3}{3.7} = \frac{20}{11.1} \approx 1.8018 \approx 1.80.$$

questions.questionTextEn: One kg of water at $27^\circ\text{C}$ is brought in contact with a heat reservoir kept at $37^\circ\text{C}$. Upon reaching thermal equilibrium, this mass of water is brought in contact with another heat reservoir kept at $47^\circ\text{C}$. The final temperature of water is $47^\circ\text{C}$. The change in entropy of the whole system in this entire process is ______ $\text{cal/K}$. (up to two decimal places) [Take specific heat at constant pressure of water as $1\text{ cal/(g K)}$]
questions.explanationEn: Convert temperatures to Kelvin: $T_0 = 27 + 273 = 300\text{ K}$, $T_1 = 37 + 273 = 310\text{ K}$, and $T_2 = 47 + 273 = 320\text{ K}$. Mass of water $m = 1\text{ kg} = 1000\text{ g}$, specific heat $c = 1\text{ cal/(g K)}$, so $mc = 1000\text{ cal/K}$. (1) Entropy change of water from $T_0$ to $T_2$: $$\Delta S_{\text{water}} = mc \ln\left(\frac{T_2}{T_0}\right) = 1000 \ln\left(\frac{320}{300}\right) = 1000 \times 0.0645385 = 64.5385\text{ cal/K}.$$ (2) Entropy change of Reservoir 1 (loses heat $Q_1 = mc(T_1 - T_0)$ at constant $T_1 = 310\text{ K}$): $$\Delta S_{\text{res},1} = -\frac{1000(310 - 300)}{310} = -\frac{10000}{310} = -32.2581\text{ cal/K}.$$ (3) Entropy change of Reservoir 2 (loses heat $Q_2 = mc(T_2 - T_1)$ at constant $T_2 = 320\text{ K}$): $$\Delta S_{\text{res},2} = -\frac{1000(320 - 310)}{320} = -\frac{10000}{320} = -31.2500\text{ cal/K}.$$ Total entropy change of the universe (whole system): $$\Delta S_{\text{total}} = 64.5385 - 32.2581 - 31.2500 = 1.0305\text{ cal/K} \approx 1.03\text{ cal/K}.$$

questions.questionTextEn: Consider a vector $\mathbf{F} = \frac{1}{\pi}\left[-\sin y\,\hat{i} + x(1 - \cos y)\,\hat{j}\right]$. The value of the integral $\oint \mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{r}$ over a circle $x^2 + y^2 = 1$ evaluated in the anti-clockwise direction is ______. (in integer)
questions.explanationEn: Apply Green's theorem in the plane for the closed anti-clockwise contour $C: x^2 + y^2 = 1$ enclosing disk $D$ of radius $1$: $$\oint_C (F_x\, dx + F_y\, dy) = \iint_D \left(\frac{\partial F_y}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial F_x}{\partial y}\right) dx\, dy.$$ Here $F_x = -\frac{1}{\pi}\sin y$ and $F_y = \frac{1}{\pi}x(1 - \cos y)$. Computing the partial derivatives: $$\frac{\partial F_y}{\partial x} = \frac{1}{\pi}(1 - \cos y), \qquad \frac{\partial F_x}{\partial y} = -\frac{1}{\pi}\cos y.$$ Subtracting gives: $$\frac{\partial F_y}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial F_x}{\partial y} = \frac{1}{\pi}(1 - \cos y + \cos y) = \frac{1}{\pi}.$$ Therefore, $\oint_C \mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{r} = \frac{1}{\pi} \times \text{Area}(D) = \frac{1}{\pi}(\pi \cdot 1^2) = 1$.

questions.topicTag: Mechanics and General Properties of Matter
questions.questionTextEn: A particle is moving with a constant angular velocity $2\text{ rad/s}$ in an orbit on a plane. The radial distance of the particle from the origin at time $t$ is given by $r = r_0 e^{2\beta t}$ where $r_0$ and $\beta$ are positive constants. The radial component of the acceleration vanishes for $\beta =$ ______ $\text{rad/s}$. (in integer)
questions.explanationEn: In plane polar coordinates, the radial component of acceleration is $a_r = \ddot{r} - r\dot{\theta}^2$. Given $\dot{\theta} = \omega = 2\text{ rad/s}$ and $r(t) = r_0 e^{2\beta t}$, we have $\dot{r} = 2\beta r_0 e^{2\beta t}$ and $\ddot{r} = 4\beta^2 r_0 e^{2\beta t} = 4\beta^2 r$. Setting $a_r = 0$: $$4\beta^2 r - r(2)^2 = 0 \implies 4\beta^2 = 4 \implies \beta^2 = 1.$$ Since $\beta$ is a positive constant, $\beta = 1\text{ rad/s}$.

questions.topicTag: Mechanics and General Properties of Matter
questions.questionTextEn: A planet rotates in an elliptical orbit with a star situated at one of the foci. The distance from the center of the ellipse to any foci is half of the semi-major axis. The ratio of the speed of the planet when it is nearest (perihelion) to the star to that at the farthest (aphelion) is ______. (in integer)
questions.explanationEn: The distance from the center of an ellipse to either focus is $ae$, where $a$ is the semi-major axis and $e$ is the eccentricity. Given $ae = \frac{a}{2}$, we get $e = \frac{1}{2}$. The perihelion and aphelion distances from the star are $r_p = a(1 - e)$ and $r_a = a(1 + e)$. By conservation of angular momentum about the star ($m v_p r_p = m v_a r_a$): $$\frac{v_p}{v_a} = \frac{r_a}{r_p} = \frac{1 + e}{1 - e} = \frac{1 + 0.5}{1 - 0.5} = \frac{1.5}{0.5} = 3.$$

questions.questionTextEn: A light beam given by $\mathbf{E}(z,t) = E_{01}\sin(kz - \omega t)\hat{i} + E_{02}\sin\left(kz - \omega t + \frac{\pi}{6}\right)\hat{j}$ passes through an ideal linear polarizer whose transmission axis is tilted by $60^\circ$ from $x$-axis (in $x$-$y$ plane). If $E_{01} = 4\text{ V/m}$ and $E_{02} = 2\text{ V/m}$, the electric field amplitude of the emerging light beam from the polarizer is ______ $\text{V/m}$. (up to two decimal places)
questions.explanationEn: The unit vector along the polarizer's transmission axis is $\hat{u} = \cos 60^\circ\,\hat{i} + \sin 60^\circ\,\hat{j} = \frac{1}{2}\hat{i} + \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\hat{j}$. Projecting $\mathbf{E}(z,t)$ onto $\hat{u}$ gives the transmitted electric field (writing $\phi = kz - \omega t$): $$E_{\text{out}} = \mathbf{E}\cdot\hat{u} = \left(4 \cdot \frac{1}{2}\right)\sin\phi + \left(2 \cdot \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)\sin\left(\phi + \frac{\pi}{6}\right) = 2\sin\phi + \sqrt{3}\sin\left(\phi + \frac{\pi}{6}\right).$$ The resultant amplitude of two harmonic oscillations of amplitudes $A = 2$, $B = \sqrt{3}$, and phase difference $\delta = \frac{\pi}{6}$ is: $$E_{\text{amp}} = \sqrt{A^2 + B^2 + 2AB\cos\delta} = \sqrt{2^2 + (\sqrt{3})^2 + 2(2)(\sqrt{3})\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)} = \sqrt{4 + 3 + 6} = \sqrt{13} \approx 3.61\text{ V/m}.$$

questions.questionTextEn: A wedge-shaped thin film is formed using soap-water solution. The refractive index of the film is $1.25$. At near normal incidence, when the film is illuminated by a monochromatic light of wavelength $600\text{ nm}$, $10$ interference fringes per $\text{cm}$ are observed. The wedge angle (in radians) is ______ $\times 10^{-5}$. (in integer)
questions.explanationEn: For a thin wedge-shaped film of refractive index $n = 1.25$ and small wedge angle $\theta$ at near-normal incidence, the fringe width is $\beta = \frac{\lambda}{2n\theta}$. Since $10$ fringes are observed per $\text{cm}$, the fringe width is $\beta = \frac{1\text{ cm}}{10} = 0.1\text{ cm} = 10^{-3}\text{ m}$. Solving for $\theta$ with $\lambda = 600\text{ nm} = 6 \times 10^{-7}\text{ m}$: $$\theta = \frac{\lambda}{2n\beta} = \frac{6 \times 10^{-7}}{2 \times 1.25 \times 10^{-3}} = \frac{6 \times 10^{-7}}{2.5 \times 10^{-3}} = 2.4 \times 10^{-4}\text{ rad} = 24 \times 10^{-5}\text{ rad}.$$ Hence, the required integer value is $24$.

questions.topicTag: Solid State Physics, Devices and Electronics
questions.questionTextEn: In an orthorhombic crystal, the lattice constants are $3.0\text{ \AA}$, $3.2\text{ \AA}$, and $4.0\text{ \AA}$. The distance $d_{101}$ between the successive $(101)$ planes is ______ $\text{\AA}$. (up to one decimal place)
questions.explanationEn: For an orthorhombic crystal with lattice constants $a = 3.0\text{ \AA}$, $b = 3.2\text{ \AA}$, and $c = 4.0\text{ \AA}$, the interplanar spacing for planes $(hkl)$ is given by: $$\frac{1}{d_{hkl}^2} = \frac{h^2}{a^2} + \frac{k^2}{b^2} + \frac{l^2}{c^2}.$$ For $(h,k,l) = (1,0,1)$: $$\frac{1}{d_{101}^2} = \frac{1^2}{(3.0)^2} + \frac{0^2}{(3.2)^2} + \frac{1^2}{(4.0)^2} = \frac{1}{9} + \frac{1}{16} = \frac{25}{144} \implies d_{101} = \frac{12}{5} = 2.4\text{ \AA}.$$

questions.questionTextEn: Consider a chamber at room temperature ($27^\circ\text{C}$) filled with a gas having a molecular diameter of $0.35\text{ nm}$. The pressure (in Pascal) to which the chamber needs to be evacuated so that the molecules have a mean free path of $1\text{ km}$ is ______ $\times 10^{-5}\text{ Pa}$. (up to two decimal places) (Boltzmann constant $k_B = 1.38 \times 10^{-23}\text{ J/K}$)
questions.explanationEn: The mean free path $\lambda$ of ideal gas molecules of diameter $d$ at temperature $T$ and pressure $P$ is: $$\lambda = \frac{k_B T}{\sqrt{2}\,\pi d^2 P} \implies P = \frac{k_B T}{\sqrt{2}\,\pi d^2 \lambda}.$$ Substituting $T = 27 + 273 = 300\text{ K}$, $d = 0.35\text{ nm} = 0.35 \times 10^{-9}\text{ m}$, $\lambda = 1\text{ km} = 10^3\text{ m}$, and $k_B = 1.38 \times 10^{-23}\text{ J/K}$: $$P = \frac{1.38 \times 10^{-23} \times 300}{\sqrt{2} \times \pi \times (0.35 \times 10^{-9})^2 \times 10^3} = \frac{4.14 \times 10^{-21}}{5.4424 \times 10^{-16}} \approx 7.607 \times 10^{-6}\text{ Pa} = 0.76 \times 10^{-5}\text{ Pa}.$$ Hence, the required value is $0.76$ (within the official accepted range $0.7$ to $1.2$).
